# Meaning Across Senses: Many Views, One Space {#sec-ch-meaning-across-senses}

The dog of the Prologue arrives as a photograph, as a word, as a bark and as a gait, and the claim of this property is that all of them can land in one neighbourhood of one space. Firth's company is a company of words. Harnad asks what grounds a symbol in something other than other symbols [@harnad1990symbol], Bender and Koller argue that a system trained on form alone has no way to learn meaning [@bender2020climbing], and Gärdenfors places meanings in spaces of qualities that the senses supply [@gardenfors2000conceptual]. The question of this chapter has two halves that the earlier plan did not separate. Does adding a sense improve the representation of meaning itself? And what else does it improve?

The scope is several senses in one space. How a reference is fixed, and whether a picture does it better than a word, is the chapter on truth (@sec-ch-meaning-and-truth). The nearness of an image to its caption, which the loss builds in, is the chapter on nearness (@sec-ch-likeness-as-nearness); the comparison of two spaces up to a change of coordinates is the chapter on arrangement (@sec-ch-meaning-as-arrangement); composition across senses is partly the chapter on composition (@sec-ch-meaning-as-composition).

*Goals and expectations (proposed, to be confirmed by the author before any experiment).*

*Goal 1, does a second sense improve meaning?* The expectation is that a text model whose vectors were shaped by images agrees better with human similarity judgments on concrete words than a text-only model of the same size, and not on abstract words, since SimLex-999 carries a concreteness rating for each of its words. The run compares the text tower of an open image-text model with a text-only space on the concrete and the abstract pairs of SimLex-999, with a bootstrap over pairs and the seed noise as the floor (@sec-sens-improve). The argument against is that an image is also form, so Bender and Koller's argument and Kripke's chain apply to a picture as much as to a word; this chapter measures an improvement and does not claim grounding.

*Goal 2, what else improves.* The expectation is that the gains of a shared space are in retrieval across modalities, in zero-shot classification and in the alignment of pairs never seen together (a sound and a word, through images), and not in composition, where models score far below people on a test of the order of words [@radford2021learning; @thrush2022winoground]. The run reproduces one retrieval and one zero-shot result with an open model and one composition failure (@sec-sens-improve).

*Goal 3, a shared space loses what is specific to a view.* A contrastive objective keeps what the views share and discards what is specific to each, and the information it can certify is bounded by the logarithm of the number of alternatives. The expectation is that the toy alignment of digits and their names reaches a ceiling set by that bound (@sec-toy-digits-names, @sec-what-shared-space-loses).

*Goal 4, the modality gap and convergence.* In image-text models the two modalities occupy separate regions of the space [@liang2022modalitygap]; whether separately trained models converge to one geometry is claimed [@huh2024platonic] and disputed, the apparent convergence of global measures largely disappearing after calibration while agreement on local neighbourhoods remains [@groger2026aristotelian; @koepke2026plato]. The run measures the gap, and the overlap of neighbours across modalities, on an open model (@sec-modality-gap, @sec-do-senses-converge).

## What the Philosophies Say About Many Senses {#sec-sens-philosophy}
*Plan (about 3 pages). The old question whether touch and sight yield one concept [@locke1694essay; @held2011newly]; grounding [@harnad1990symbol] and the argument from form [@bender2020climbing]; Kripke's chain, in which a name is tied to its bearer by a history that a picture does not carry by itself [@kripke1980naming]; Gärdenfors's quality spaces [@gardenfors2000conceptual]; and Chomsky's distinction between I-language, the system in the speaker's head, and E-language, the corpus of what is said: a text model is trained on E-language only, and a multimodal one adds the senses but not the head. For each account, what a vector carries of it and where it stops.*

## Does a Second Sense Help? {#sec-sens-improve}
*Plan (about 4 pages). Goals 1 and 2. The text tower of an open image-text model against a text-only space on SimLex-999 by concreteness; retrieval and zero-shot classification from an open model; the composition failure on a swap test. Null: the seed gap and a text-only model of the same size. The claims that a second sense improves robustness or data efficiency are not assumed: they are listed here as claims without a source in the collection.*


<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/multimodal_embeddings.qmd, section sec-grounding-problem -->
## The Grounding Problem {#sec-grounding-problem}
*Firth's company is a company of words. Harnad's symbol grounding, Bender and Koller's argument that form alone does not yield meaning, and Gärdenfors's conceptual spaces, set against the dog test of the Prologue: what would a photograph, the word, a bark, and a gait have to share? Chomsky's distinction (1986) between I-language, the system in the speaker's head, and E-language, the corpus of what is said: a text model is trained on E-language only, and a multimodal one adds the senses but not the head.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/multimodal_embeddings.qmd, section sec-meaning-what-views-share -->
## Meaning as What Views Share {#sec-meaning-what-views-share}
*A working definition of the semantic content of a signal as the information shared by different views of the same cause, which is Shannon's mutual information between channels. Told as a historical sequence: CCA (1936), deep CCA and DeViSE (2013), natural pairs such as the frames and the audio track of a video (2017), and CLIP (2021) as InfoNCE across modalities, whose optimum relates to the pointwise mutual information between an image and its caption, the cross-modal counterpart of the word-context PMI of @sec-ch-likeness-as-nearness.*

## One Hub, Many Modalities {#sec-one-hub-many-modalities}
*How binding every modality to images (ImageBind, 2023) aligns pairs that were never seen together, such as audio and text, and what that suggests about the shared structure of the senses.*

## Two Routes to One Space {#sec-two-routes-one-space}
*Separate encoders aligned by a contrastive loss versus a single transformer over interleaved tokens (@sec-ch-meaning-in-context), with post-hoc alignment (@sec-ch-meaning-as-arrangement) as a third, and what each route keeps and loses.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/multimodal_embeddings.qmd, section sec-toy-digits-names -->
## A Toy Alignment: Digits and Their Names {#sec-toy-digits-names}
*Plan (1–2 pages). The first multimodal experiment, moved from the InfoNCE section of @sec-ch-likeness-as-nearness. Images of the 8×8 digits on one side, with the encoder of that chapter, and the number words "zero" to "nine" on the other, as one-hot vectors followed by a linear map (a lookup table), with the same symmetric InfoNCE loss and two different encoders. The result is the 10×10 matrix of cosines between the mean image vector of each digit and the ten word vectors, and top-1 accuracy of the image against the words. With only $m = 10$ kinds of positive the batch must have $k \ll m$: random batches against batches with one image per word ($k = 9$), and $k = 127$ as the counter-example, where about 13 alternatives share the label of the anchor, the loss cannot go below its floor and the bound is capped at $\log_2 10 = 3.3$ bits.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/multimodal_embeddings.qmd, section sec-what-shared-space-loses -->
## What a Shared Space Loses {#sec-what-shared-space-loses}
*A contrastive objective keeps what the views share and discards what is specific to one of them, and the InfoNCE estimate of mutual information cannot exceed $\log_2(k+1)$ for $k$ alternatives per positive. The fur texture of the dog is not in its bark.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/multimodal_embeddings.qmd, section sec-modality-gap -->
## The Modality Gap {#sec-modality-gap}
*Why embeddings of different modalities occupy separate cones even after contrastive training, its relation to the anisotropy of @sec-ch-likeness-as-nearness and the hubness of Chapters [-@sec-ch-curse-of-dimensionality] and [-@sec-ch-likeness-as-nearness], and what it means for the claim of a "single" space.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/multimodal_embeddings.qmd, section sec-predicting-space-signal -->
## Predicting in the Space, Not the Signal {#sec-predicting-space-signal}
*Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA), which predict the embedding of a masked or future part of a signal from the embedding of its context, so that the views are context and target within one signal rather than two modalities. The prediction of embeddings of @sec-ch-likeness-as-nearness, now applied where it was designed to matter: a generative model must spend capacity on every pixel, a latent predictor can ignore what it cannot predict. The debate between the two is taken up in the closing section of @sec-ch-meaning-as-generation; this chapter tells the image, video and planning forms. Told as a historical sequence: LeCun's position paper on autonomous machine intelligence (2022); I-JEPA for images (2023); V-JEPA for video (2024); and V-JEPA 2 (2025), whose action-conditioned predictor plans in latent space. A world model is a learned map from a state and an action to the next state, a discrete vector field on the embedding manifold, and planning is the search for a trajectory along it (@sec-ch-meaning-as-path), which is where the agentic trajectories of the Prologue live. The question of @sec-ch-meaning-in-context, whether thinking can stay in the space instead of passing through text, is here asked of planning, where latent rollouts have a longer record: world models (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Dreamer) and diffusion planners (Diffuser, 2022). The link to predictive processing in the brain is taken up in the Epilogue.*

<!-- salvaged from embedding-technologies-stubs/multimodal_embeddings.qmd, section sec-composition-across-senses -->
## Composition Across Senses {#sec-composition-across-senses}
*Binding attributes to objects across modalities (Chapters [-@sec-ch-meaning-as-composition] and [-@sec-ch-meaning-as-composition]), and the failures that remain. Winoground pairs two captions with the same words in another order with two images: people reach 89.5, 88.5 and 85.5 on the text, image and group scores, and the best of the models tested 38.0, 20.5 and 14.5 (chance 25, 25 and 16.7) [@thrush2022winoground]; the same swap-based probe is run on the sentence encoders of @sec-ch-likeness-as-nearness.*

## Images, Sounds and Video {#sec-likeness-images-sounds-video}
*What the human judges of the other levels say (read in the PDFs; none was run here). The section had no human judge for images and sounds, and they exist. (1) Peterson, Abbott and Griffiths (2018 [@peterson2018evaluating]) compare the similarity implied by networks trained on ImageNet with human ratings over six sets of natural images: the variance explained by the raw representations ($R^2$) is 0.58 for animals, 0.51 automobiles, 0.37 "various", 0.27 fruits, 0.27 vegetables and 0.19 furniture, against a human inter-rater reliability between 0.57 and 0.90; a linear reweighting of the feature dimensions learned from the ratings roughly doubles it (0.84 for animals, 0.67 for furniture), and with cross-validation as control 0.74 and 0.35, but a transformation learned on one category does not transfer well to another (for example $R^2$ of 0.02 to 0.25 from animals or fruits to the others). It is Goodman's problem in numbers: the weights of the respects are those of the domain (@sec-likeness-which). (2) Muttenthaler et al. (2023 [@muttenthaler2023human]) use the odd-one-out task of THINGS, with a maximum achievable accuracy of 67.2 per cent, and find that scale and architecture "have essentially no effect" on alignment with human judgements, whereas the training objective and the dataset matter more, that image-text and larger diverse datasets help, that a linear transformation learned on one human dataset improves two others, and that food and animals are well represented and royal or sports-related objects are not: scaling alone is unlikely to be enough. (3) Zhang et al. (2018 [@zhang2018unreasonable]) find on a dataset of human two-alternative judgements that deep features beat the classical pixel and structure metrics by wide margins whatever the architecture and the level of supervision (supervised, self-supervised or unsupervised), so that "perceptual similarity is an emergent property shared across deep visual representations"; Fu et al. (2023 [@fu2023dreamsim]) show that these metrics miss mid-level similarity (layout, pose, content) and tune a metric on 20,000 synthetic triplets that reaches 96.2 per cent agreement with human choices on its own set. (4) Marjieh et al. (2022 [@marjieh2022words]) evaluate 611 pretrained models on human similarity judgements of images, audio and video and find a large gap to the human judgements (the split-half reliability being the ceiling), and a better prediction from the embeddings of text descriptions (tags, captions) than from the vision, audio or video models, with a correlation of 0.74 for the best tag-based method on one set against 0.64 for the best method on the dataset labels; and a language model asked directly for the pairwise judgement reproduces human data across six modalities, recovering the colour wheel and the pitch spiral (Marjieh et al. 2023 [@marjieh2023large]). The consequence is that, for modalities other than text, a text description is already a good stand-in for likeness, and a caption-trained space gets its likeness partly through the words. (5) Sound: CLAP (Elizalde et al. 2023 [@elizalde2023clap]; Wu et al. 2023 [@wu2023large]) trains audio and text encoders with a contrastive loss on pairs, and classifies a sound zero-shot by the cosine between the audio embedding and the text embedding of each class name, so audio-to-text nearness is built in (the paired cell of the final table) while audio-to-audio nearness is the emergent cell and is not reported as such in the parts read. (6) Time: Wei et al. (2018 [@wei2018learning]) train a network to tell whether a video plays forwards or backwards, reaching about 80 per cent on large real-video benchmarks and, on the Reverse Film set, 76 and 72 per cent for the two pretrainings against 80 per cent for people (their Table 9), and show that black frames and camera motion are shortcuts (removing them lowers the accuracy by about 10 points each); so the question "is a clip played backwards near the forward one" is a question about how much of the clip is direction and how much is an artefact, and a space trained with forward-only pairs cannot say.*

*What is near when the training signal is a label, an augmentation or a caption: the same class, the same content under a change, the same description. A pair-level statistic works for a categorical judge (the chance of ranking a same-class pair above a different-class pair, 0.5 under the null). A bark against other barks and against a doorbell. In video, time is a new question: is a clip played backwards near the forward one, and should it be?*

## Technologies That Exploit Many Senses {#sec-sens-technologies}
*Plan (about 1 page). Image-text and audio-text models, one-hub models that bind many modalities to images, joint-embedding predictive architectures, and multimodal retrieval. For each: the cost of the encoders, whether the alignment improves with scale or the gap and the loss of modality-specific information persist as the structure of the problem, and whether the evidence at scale supports the claim.*

## Does the Dog Look the Same? {#sec-does-dog-look-same}
*Plan (1 page). Findings: what a shared space keeps (what the views share) and loses (what is specific to each sense), the modality gap, how weak the dynamics are, and what composition across senses still fails to do. Achieved for the representation of meaning: several senses in one space (@sec-prop-senses). This chapter gives its own answer to the dog test, with what is lost; the Epilogue collects the answers of all the chapters. Computation: does scale make the alignment between modalities easier, or do the modality gap, the loss of modality-specific information and the failure of composition persist as the structure of the problem? And does prediction in latent space scale as a general method, as its proponents argue against autoregressive generation, or is it a prior that scaled generative models will absorb (the debate of the closing section of @sec-ch-meaning-as-generation)? Evidence at scale: CLIP, trained on 400 million image-text pairs, is the held comparison of a contrastive objective against predicting the caption (Radford et al., Figure 2: the contrastive objective about 4 times more efficient than a bag-of-words predictor, which was itself about 3 times more efficient than a caption transformer), and it is the authors' own. The modality gap and the convergence claims are single-study or contested, and the chapter states N, scale and status in the same sentence. Smoke test: the digits experiment of @sec-ch-likeness-as-nearness with a different encoder for each view, measuring the offset (a column of its contrast table) as a small analogue of the modality gap. Still out of reach: whether any of this is meaning and not only structure, which the Epilogue takes up.*

*Sources and gaps (first pass).* Sourced in `references/`: grounding, the argument from form, quality spaces, the modality gap, the convergence claim and its sceptics, contrastive image-text training, Winoground. Not yet sourced: the claim that a second sense improves the agreement of text vectors with human similarity judgments on concrete words (a result of the multimodal distributional semantics literature, from memory, not in the collection); the claims about robustness and data efficiency; the figures of the earlier closing section are those of the earlier chapter.
